questions.question: What is a combination?
options: An ordered arrangement of all elements
A selection of $k$ elements, ignoring order
A probability assigned to a single outcome.
A sequence in which repetition is required

questions.question: When are combinations used?
options: When ranking positions matters
When only the chosen group matters
When every outcome must be ordered by time
When all events are disjoint

questions.question: What is the standard count of $k$-combinations from $n$ distinct objects?
options: $\binom nk$
$n^k$
$n+k$

questions.question: How do combinations and permutations differ?
options: Combinations count order, while permutations ignore order
Combinations require repeated elements, while permutations forbid finite sets
Combinations ignore order, while permutations count order
Combinations apply only to probabilities, while permutations apply only to events

questions.question: Which notation commonly represents the number of combinations?
options: $n/k$
$n\cap k$
$\binom nk$

questions.question: Choosing three committee members from twelve people is counted by what?
options: A permutation of all twelve people
A combination
A complement only
A probability density

questions.question: A five-card poker hand is counted as a combination because what does not matter?
options: The order of the cards in the hand
The identities of the cards
The number of cards selected
Whether the sample space is finite

questions.question: How many ways are there to choose $2$ spare parts from $10$ distinct parts?
How many ways are there to choose $2$ people from $4$ people, ignoring order?
Which situation is best modeled by a combination?
options: Assigning gold, silver, and bronze medals
Listing books from left to right on a shelf
Selecting $4$ students for an unordered project group
Creating a password where position matters

questions.question: Why do combinations avoid overcounting unordered selections?
options: They count each ordering separately
Rearrangements of chosen objects are one selection
They require every object to be selected.
They exclude all finite sets

questions.question: What assumption is included in 'selecting $k$ elements from $A$' when $A$ has $n$ elements and $k\le n$?
options: The selection size cannot exceed the available elements
Order must be recorded for every selected element.
The set $A$ must be infinite
The selected elements must all be identical

questions.question: Why is a committee without roles a combination rather than a permutation?
options: Changing the order of the listed members does not change the committee
The committee members must be chosen in a timeline
Every committee has a first, second, and third position
Combinations are used whenever people are involved

questions.question: How many unordered pairs can be chosen from $5$ distinct objects?
From $8$ people, how many unordered teams of $3$ can be formed?
options: $\binom83$

questions.question: Which pair represents the same combination when choosing letters?
options: $ABC$ and $ABD$
$A$ and $B$

questions.question: Why is $\binom nk$ smaller than $n!/(n-k)!$ when $1<k<n$?
options: The combination count allows repeated elements
The permutation count distinguishes the $k!$ orders of each chosen group
The permutation count ignores order while the combination count records it
The two counts are always equal for finite sets

questions.question: Which modeling detail would change a combination problem into a permutation problem?
options: Forgetting the names of all selected objects
Checking that $k\le n$
Using a finite set instead of an infinite set
Giving the selected positions distinct roles or ranks

questions.question: A club chooses a president, secretary, and treasurer from $10$ people. Why is this not counted by $\binom{10}{3}$?
options: The selection has more than $10$ people
The distinct roles make the same people different outcomes
Committees can never be counted by combinations.
The problem has no finite sample space
